title: Asking for What You Want Is an Essential Skill
author: Molly Graham
summary: Graham opens with a former boss who told her he had never had to ask for a promotion, a remark that left her ashamed and that she now sees as a damaging message. She argues that good work often does not speak for itself, and that being good at a job and being good at advocating for yourself are two separate skills. Drawing on her WorkLife podcast conversation with lawyer Wendy Chow, she says people wrongly treat asking as a personality trait when it is a practiced skill. Three ideas follow: use a grumpy wish list, built from what you complain about on bad days, to find what to ask for; give people a reason to say yes with a merit-based ask supported by two data points; and make it easy to say yes by timing the ask, giving notice and treating the boss as a partner. She closes that it is your place to ask, and that you should not feel ashamed for doing so.
points: Doing the job well and advocating for yourself are different skills, so strong work alone will not secure promotions, pay or opportunities.
Asking is a practiced skill rather than a personality trait, so lack of ease is a sign of too little practice.
A grumpy wish list, built from worst-day complaints, turns frustrations into concrete requests for resources, projects, flexibility, training or responsibility.
A merit-based ask needs only two relevant data points explaining why the request makes sense.
Make yes easy by timing the ask to the company's rhythms, giving advance notice and helping the boss build the case for approvers.
quotes: But being good at your job and being good at advocating for yourself are two completely different, equally important skills.
Wendy thinks part of the reason we’re so bad at advocating for ourselves is that we treat it as a personality trait. We assume some people are naturally good at it and other people aren’t.
Instead of imagining your dream job on your very best day at work, think about what you complain about on your worst days.
Those frustrations are information. And they’re often the beginnings of a list of things you could actually ask to change.
Wendy says you’d be surprised how often people work up the courage to ask for something and then don’t actually explain why they should get it.
Wendy believes you often only need TWO data points to make a credible case. Not an enormous spreadsheet. Not months of research. Two relevant pieces of evidence.
Instead of making it you versus them, ask what they would need to help make it happen. And then help them make your case.
You might not always get what you want. And yes, you should learn how to make a thoughtful, well-timed, well-supported ask. But you shouldn’t have to feel ashamed for asking.
context: Merit alone does not guarantee recognition, so advocacy is a separate skill.
Reframing asking as practice makes it learnable in the author's argument.
Worst-day complaints point to what is worth requesting in the author's argument.
Frustrations can be converted into specific asks beyond salary.
A request without a reason gives the listener nothing to say yes to.
A credible case is small and specific, not exhaustive in the author's argument.
Treating the boss as a partner lowers resistance and arms them with an argument.
The closing message is that asking is legitimate and no cause for shame.
